caption:
Google just made its Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash video model generally available.
Clips now run up to 15 seconds, up from 10, and you can edit them by chatting instead of starting over.
In Google Vids, anyone with a Google account can make up to three 15-second videos a month for free.

What would you make with a free 15-second AI video?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: The Next Web, The Decoder · Photo: Google
threads_text: Google's Gemini Omni video model now makes 15-second clips, and Google Vids lets anyone with a Google account make three of them a month for free. You can also fix a clip by just telling it what to change. Would you use free AI video for anything real?

site_article.headline: Google makes Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash available with 15-second videos and lower prices
site_article.dek: Anyone with a Google account can make three free 15-second clips a month in Google Vids, while the Gemini app version goes to Ultra subscribers first.
site_article.summary: Google made its Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash video model generally available on November 5, 2026, raising the clip limit from 10 to 15 seconds and adding editing by follow-up instructions. API pricing fell 30 percent to about $0.07 per second of 720p video.
site_article.seo_title: Google Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: 15-second AI videos, lower price
site_article.seo_description: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash makes 3 to 15 second videos, adds conversational editing, costs about $0.07 per second and gives Vids users three free clips a month.
site_article.answer_summary: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is Google's updated AI video model. It makes clips of up to 15 seconds, lets users edit them through follow-up instructions, and is free for up to three clips a month in Google Vids.

paragraphs.text: Google made Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, its video generation model, generally available on November 5, 2026, according to The Next Web and The Decoder. The update raises the maximum clip length from 10 seconds to 15 seconds, adds editing through follow-up instructions and lowers the price developers pay for each second of video.

Google first showed Omni Flash at its I/O conference in May 2026, when clips were capped at 10 seconds, The Next Web reported. Fone Arena reported that clips can now be set anywhere from 3 to 15 seconds in one-second steps.
The broadest access comes through Google Vids. According to Fone Arena, anyone with a Google account or a Workspace subscription can make up to three 15-second videos per month in Vids at no cost.

In the Gemini app, 15-second videos are rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers, The Next Web and Fone Arena reported. The model is also rolling out in Flow and in Google Ads for video campaigns. Developers can reach it through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, and businesses through Google Cloud, which The Next Web said is the first time Omni has been generally available there.

The main new feature is what Google calls conversational editing. Instead of generating a clip again from scratch, a user can refine the same video over several turns, for example by swapping a product or a background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio, according to Fone Arena and The Decoder. The Decoder reported that Google says these edits work across the full 15 seconds.

The model accepts several kinds of references at once: images of characters, product photos, style images, short motion clips of up to 3 seconds and audio cues, The Decoder reported. Google says faces, clothing, packaging text and brand colors stay more consistent across camera angles. One demo cited by The Decoder builds a 15-second virtual try-on sequence with 360-degree turns from a single model photo and three product shots of outfits.

Google also points to more natural dialogue with clearer lip-sync, support for several speakers, and continuous camera moves such as drone flythroughs and zoom-outs with fewer jump cuts. In Google DeepMind's own comparisons, testers preferred version 1.2 over version 1.1 for visual consistency 62 percent of the time, The Next Web reported.

Through the Gemini API, 720p video now costs about $0.07 per second, a 30 percent cut from $0.10 per second in June, according to The Next Web. Fone Arena and The Decoder reported that users can save more by drafting at 360p or 720p and upscaling only the final clips to 1080p or 4K. Every generated video carries an invisible SynthID watermark.

Google acknowledged that work continues on fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics, The Next Web and Fone Arena reported. The Next Web also noted that ByteDance's Seedance 2.5, shown in June, already makes 30-second clips, and that Google is the only US company in the top 10 of one popular AI video ranking, with Chinese models holding the other nine places.

The free tier in Google Vids is the part most people will notice. Three short clips a month is a small allowance, but it puts a current Google video model in front of ordinary account holders rather than only paying subscribers and developers. The lower API price and the edit-instead-of-regenerate approach point the same way: Google is trying to make AI video cheaper to iterate on, which matters most for advertisers and small teams that make many versions of the same clip.
Watch whether Google extends 15-second generation from Ultra to cheaper Gemini plans, and whether it can close the gap with 30-second rivals such as Seedance 2.5.
